items.prompt:
Read this paragraph and list everything that needs to be revised. Then rewrite it.

'My dog is nice. He does stuff. He is good. Dogs are animals. I also like cats.'
items.answer: Problems: 'nice,' 'stuff,' and 'good' are vague; 'Dogs are animals' is obvious and does not add information; 'I also like cats' is off topic. Revised: 'My golden retriever, Buddy, is one of the friendliest dogs I have ever met. He runs to greet me every day after school and brings me his favorite squeaky toy as a gift. Buddy also knows three tricks: sit, shake, and roll over, which always makes visitors laugh.'

steps: Replace vague words with specific details.
Remove the obvious fact and the off-topic sentence.
Add specific examples of what the dog does.

items.prompt: Your classmate wrote: 'I like science class. We do experiments. It is my favorite subject.' Your teacher asks you to give peer feedback. Write three specific questions that would help your classmate improve the paragraph.
items.answer: Question 1: What kind of experiments do you do? Can you give a specific example? Question 2: What do you learn from the experiments? Question 3: Why is science your favorite subject rather than another class?

steps: Good peer feedback asks specific questions that guide the writer to add details.
Ask about what, why, and how to push the writer to explain more.

items.prompt:
Revise this narrative paragraph by adding details, removing one off-topic sentence, and strengthening the ending.

'One day I went to the fair. I rode rides. I like hamburgers. The fair was fun. I went home.'
items.answer: Revised: 'One hot Saturday, my dad took me to the county fair. First, I rode the spinning teacups so fast that I screamed with laughter. Then, I watched a juggler toss flaming torches into the air. Finally, we walked back to the car as the sun set, and I told my dad it was the best day of the year.'

steps: Remove 'I like hamburgers' — off topic.
Add details to each event (spinning teacups, juggler).
Replace 'I went home' with a strong closing that shows feeling.

items.prompt: A student's teacher wrote this feedback on her paper: 'Your opening sentence is strong, but your middle loses focus and your ending does not match your beginning.' Explain what each piece of feedback means and what the student should do.
items.answer: Strong opening: no change needed. Middle loses focus: check if every sentence connects to the topic. Remove sentences that wander off topic and add sentences that stay on the subject. Ending does not match beginning: reread the opening sentence and write an ending that connects back to it. For example, if the beginning says 'I love thunderstorms,' the ending should tie back to that feeling or idea.

steps: 'Loses focus' means off-topic sentences appeared. Fix: remove them.
'Ending does not match' means the closing does not connect back to the main idea. Fix: rewrite the ending to reference the opening topic.

items.prompt:
Revise this informative paragraph to make every sentence more specific and detailed.

'Spiders are animals. They catch bugs. They live in many places. Spiders are interesting.'
items.answer: Spiders are eight-legged arachnids that are found on every continent except Antarctica. They catch insects and other small creatures by spinning silk webs that trap prey when it flies or walks into them. Spiders live in a huge range of environments, from dark caves to sunny meadows to the corners of houses. Their ability to spin silk makes them one of the most unique and fascinating animals on Earth.

steps: 'Animals' → 'eight-legged arachnids found on every continent except Antarctica.'
'Catch bugs' → 'catch insects by spinning silk webs that trap prey.'
'Many places' → 'dark caves to sunny meadows to the corners of houses.'
'Interesting' → specific reason why they are fascinating.

items.prompt: Write a before-and-after revision of one sentence. Start with a weak sentence and then revise it twice to make it stronger each time.
items.answer: Draft 1 (weak): 'It was cold.' Draft 2 (better): 'The morning was cold.' Draft 3 (strong): 'The January morning was so cold that my breath turned to white fog the moment I stepped outside and my fingers went numb before I reached the bus stop.'

steps: Draft 1: no details at all.
Draft 2: adds when (morning).
Draft 3: adds month, a physical sensation (breath, fingers), and where it happened.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between editing and revising. Give one example of each.
items.answer: Revising means improving the content of writing: adding details, removing off-topic sentences, strengthening weak words, or reorganizing. Example: changing 'The dog ran' to 'The golden retriever bolted across the muddy field.' Editing means fixing errors in spelling, punctuation, and grammar. Example: changing 'the dog ran fast.' to 'The dog ran fast.'

steps: Revision = improving ideas and details.
Editing = correcting mechanical errors (spelling, capitalization, punctuation).

items.prompt:
Rewrite this weak paragraph about autumn by replacing every vague word with a specific detail:

'Fall is nice. Things change. The weather is different. I do stuff outside.'
items.answer: Autumn is one of the most beautiful seasons of the year. The leaves on maple and oak trees turn brilliant shades of red, orange, and gold before floating to the ground. The air becomes cool and crisp, carrying the smell of wood smoke and apples. I love jumping into the piles of leaves my dad rakes into the yard and crunching them under my boots.

steps: 'Nice' → specific adjective (beautiful).
'Things change' → leaves turn colors.
'Weather is different' → cool, crisp, smell of wood smoke.
'Stuff outside' → jumping in leaves, crunching under boots.

items.prompt: A student is writing about why she loves the ocean. She wrote three sentences but they are all about the same idea: 'I love the ocean. The ocean is great. The ocean is amazing.' Revise these three sentences so each one says something DIFFERENT about why she loves the ocean.
items.answer: I love the ocean because the sound of the waves makes me feel calm and peaceful. The wide, open water stretches as far as I can see and makes me feel like anything is possible. Best of all, the ocean is full of hidden creatures, from tiny crabs to giant sea turtles, waiting to be discovered.

steps: Sentence 1: emotional reason (sound, calm).
Sentence 2: visual reason (wide open space).
Sentence 3: curiosity and discovery reason.

items.prompt:
Read a classmate's paragraph and find one off-topic sentence, one vague sentence, and one strong sentence. Explain each.

'The rainforest is full of life. It is nice there. Many animals like jaguars, macaws, and poison dart frogs live there. I went to the store yesterday.'
items.answer: Off-topic: 'I went to the store yesterday.' — has nothing to do with the rainforest. Vague: 'It is nice there.' — 'nice' does not tell the reader anything specific about the rainforest. Strong: 'Many animals like jaguars, macaws, and poison dart frogs live there.' — uses specific examples that inform the reader.

steps: Off-topic sentence: does not mention the rainforest at all.
Vague sentence: uses the word 'nice' without any specific detail.
Strong sentence: names three specific animals, giving the reader real information.

items.prompt:
Write a revised version of this sentence THREE different ways, each adding a different type of detail (when, where, and how).

Original: 'She laughed.'
items.answer: When: 'At the end of the joke, she laughed.' Where: 'She laughed from her seat in the back of the classroom.' How: 'She laughed so hard that tears rolled down her cheeks and she had to hold her stomach.'

steps: Adding 'when' answers at what point it happened.
Adding 'where' places the action in a setting.
Adding 'how' describes the manner and intensity of the action.

items.prompt: A student gets this peer comment: 'I cannot tell who is in your story.' What should the writer revise?
items.answer: The writer should add the name or description of the main character near the beginning. For example, instead of 'They went to the park,' write 'My best friend Marcus and I went to the park on Saturday.'

steps: The reader cannot follow a story without knowing who the characters are.
Add a name or description early in the story.

items.prompt:
Revise this opinion paragraph by strengthening the reason and improving the closing sentence.

'I think school is important. School is good for kids. School is nice.'
items.answer: I think school is one of the most important places a child can go. School teaches students to read, write, do math, and understand the world around them, which are skills they will use for the rest of their lives. That is why every child deserves access to a good education.

steps: Replace 'good for kids' with a specific reason: what does school teach?
Replace 'School is nice' with a meaningful closing sentence.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph and decide which sentence most needs revision. Rewrite only that sentence.

'Honeybees are fascinating insects. They live in hives with thousands of other bees. They make honey. Each bee in the hive has a special job to help the whole colony survive.'
items.answer: 'They make honey' is the weakest sentence because it is too vague. Revised: 'Worker bees collect nectar from flowers and store it in the hive, where it slowly dries and thickens into sweet honey.'

steps: 'They make honey' is short and does not explain how.
Add HOW bees make honey: collecting nectar and letting it thicken.

items.prompt: Write a before version (weak, vague) and an after version (revised, specific) of a paragraph about what you did after school one day.
items.answer: Before: 'I came home. I did stuff. I ate. I went to sleep.' After: 'One Tuesday afternoon, I came home from school and dropped my backpack by the door. First, I made myself a peanut butter snack and read two chapters of my chapter book at the kitchen table. Then, I played outside with my neighbor until the streetlights came on. Finally, after dinner, I took a warm shower and fell asleep before my dad had even finished reading our bedtime story.'

steps: Before: every sentence is vague with no details.
After: adds when, what was eaten, what book, who was played with, and a sensory ending.
